<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases and answered pressure questions directly, but PRO's core asymmetry — irreversible ecological/carbon loss versus a narrower, more preventable loss of unrealized expansion income — held up better under scrutiny. PRO sharpened this in the later rounds by narrowing its restriction to new frontier permits rather than existing farms, and by identifying a concrete enforcement-mechanics distinction (a centralized, dated, auditable licensing decision versus a diffuse, hard-to-attribute fire), reinforced by external market pressure (EU rules, buyer traceability) that CON never fully neutralized. CON's rebuttals were intelligent — pressing on capture, distributional risk to undocumented smallholders, and leakage — but its own late-introduced enforcement mechanism (satellite monitoring, permit audits) ended up resembling PRO's tools without clearly outperforming them, and its claim that families "already farming" might still suffer debt/schooling harm from a merely denied future expansion felt more speculative than PRO's counter-examples. PRO's closing more effectively converted CON's "no mechanism guarantees immunity from capture" concession into a symmetry argument that favored PRO's earlier intervention point, leaving PRO with the cleaner, more resolved comparative story.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B4.1/B5.1 exchange — reframing the capture debate as "which enforcement point is more auditable" (centralized permit vs. diffuse fire) and then noting in closing that CON's "visibility doesn't force action" objection cuts equally against CON's own enforcement plan — was the most decisive turn, since CON's A4 response conceded shared capture risk without dislodging PRO's timing/chokepoint advantage.</best_rebuttal>
